synthesis: The short |zeta|^2 integral is first exposed as a mean-versus-typical problem: its t-average is asymptotic to log T, but fractional q-moments with q<1 suppress exceptional large samples and prove an upper scale with denominator sqrt(1+(1-q)log log T). The exponent-two discussion identifies this as the critical boundary where rare values begin to control the partition mass. In the proof, a high-probability multiscale good event excludes oversized partial smooth Euler products; after deterministic-to-Steinhaus transfer, an imported critical random-Euler-product estimate supplies the same renormalization. Together these sections connect the observed fractional-moment saving to a barrier-restricted critical model, without proving a zeta critical-chaos limit.
source_support: Unit u01 defines the short integral and contrasts its classical mean log T with the unknown typical size. Unit u02 proves the uniform q-moment upper bound and derives the typical/tail corollary by optimized Markov inequality. Unit u03 explains beta=1 (exponent two) as the freezing transition between collective and exceptional contributions. Unit u05 supplies the proof bridge: smooth/rough factorization, a multiscale good event, polynomial derandomization, separation of rough variance, and reuse of the earlier random critical-chaos estimate.
nonparaphrase_operation: The synthesis aligns three representations of the same scale change: a distributional probe (vary q below one), a path restriction (remove trajectories crossing partial-product barriers), and a random-model calculation (critical Euler-product mass). Their common output is the square-root log-log saving, while their epistemic roles remain different.
limits: For zeta the paper proves upper bounds, not matching lower bounds, an exact tail, or convergence to critical multiplicative chaos. The critical-chaos explanation and freezing language motivate the normalization; the decisive probabilistic estimate is imported from prior random-model work. The barrier mechanism restricts the smooth factor and averages the rough factor rather than demonstrating that every large zeta sample is removed. Fractional powers, optimized q, parameter choices, and displayed normalizations are OCR-sensitive and require the PDF for literal reuse.
quality_reason: Accepted because u01-u03 establish the critical distributional question and proved fractional-moment effect, while u05 independently explains how the proof transports a barrier-restricted random critical estimate to zeta. The relation is a concrete mechanism unavailable from any one parent and is stated without upgrading model analogy to a zeta limit theorem.

synthesis: The factorization assigns different evidential roles to different prime ranges. The P-smooth polynomial is short enough to approximate an Euler product, encode multiscale barriers, and survive Taylor expansion into bounded-length Dirichlet polynomials. The P-rough polynomial is not forced into an Euler-product representation: it remains in the product through the time-to-Steinhaus transfer and is collapsed only at the end to its second moment by prime independence. This asymmetric treatment preserves the large-prime contribution to the total log T scale that would be lost by truncating it, while exposing only the small-prime structure needed for the upper estimate.
source_support: Unit u11 proves a mean-square approximation of the approximate-functional-equation polynomial by separated P-smooth and P-rough factors of shortened total length. Unit u09 supplies the diagonal/orthogonality mean-value bridge to Steinhaus expectations. Unit u17 polynomializes the smooth barrier majorants and applies that bridge while retaining both factors; the reconstructed random expectation still contains the rough sum. Unit u05 and the explicit comparison in u07 then use independence to replace the rough square by a variance of order log T/log P and contrast this with methods that discard large primes and detect a smaller scale.
nonparaphrase_operation: Treat the proof as an information-budget decomposition: preserve phase-sensitive multiscale data only where it is usable (the smooth factor), preserve scale but forget phase for the rough factor (its variance), and check that the two losses occur at different stages rather than deleting the rough range at the outset.
limits: The smooth/rough product is an average approximation, not a pointwise factorization of zeta, and the deterministic-to-random replacement requires strict polynomial-length and Taylor-error bounds. The final rough-factor reduction retains energy but loses localization and concentration data, so it is adapted to upper averages and does not support a converse or a matching maximum lower bound. Exact cutoffs, epsilon and P powers, lengths, and error terms are severely OCR/formula-sensitive.
quality_reason: Accepted because u11, u09, and u17 jointly verify the factorization-transfer pipeline, while u07 supplies the explicit methodological comparison showing why retaining the rough factor preserves scale. This is a source-supported representation strategy rather than a generic small-primes/large-primes theme.

synthesis: The derandomization is ordered around a probabilistic restriction rather than an unconditional Euler-product replacement. First the proof defines a simultaneous multiscale good event and uses optimized even moments plus a union bound to make its failure rare. Only on that restricted region are interval indicators replaced by smooth band-limited majorants, Taylor-truncated into bounded-degree polynomials, and combined with the smooth/rough Dirichlet product. Length-controlled mean-value orthogonality then converts the deterministic t-average into a Steinhaus expectation; independence removes the rough variance, and an imported random critical-Euler-product bound controls the remaining smooth restricted mass.
source_support: Unit u13 defines the multiscale event and reduces Theorem 1 to a restricted average plus a bad-event estimate. Units u10 and u15 give the even-moment tool and its optimized union-bound application proving rarity of barrier failure. Unit u12 constructs the smooth majorant with derivative control needed for polynomial approximation. Unit u17 performs the Taylor expansion, bounds its remainders under length constraints, applies mean-value orthogonality, and reconstructs the random event. Unit u16 factors off the rough second moment by independence and invokes the prior random estimate.
nonparaphrase_operation: The synthesis type-checks the proof pipeline: path predicate -> smooth functional -> finite Dirichlet polynomial -> diagonal time average -> random expectation -> independent smooth and rough components. Reversing the first two steps would be invalid because a raw simultaneous indicator is not directly available to the mean-value lemma.
limits: The final critical random estimate comes from earlier work and is not proved in these units. Success depends on a delicate ledger linking Taylor degree, P, epsilon, total Dirichlet length, union-bound mesh, and remainder sizes; the extracted formulas are fragmented enough that exact inequalities and constants need PDF verification. The procedure proves an upper bound on a restricted average plus a rare exceptional set, not an equality in law between zeta and a Steinhaus model.
quality_reason: Accepted because six distinct units support successive indispensable bridges, including why the barrier must precede polynomialization. The synthesis adds a concrete ordering constraint and proof-burden map rather than merely restating that derandomization occurs.

synthesis: A pointwise maximum is converted through two controlled information losses into a path event suitable for an upper bound. Cauchy's formula places the unknown maximizing value inside a 1/log T rectangle and bounds it by contour integrals that can be averaged. After smooth/rough approximation, a restricted fourth-moment estimate shows in measure that contributions with a small smooth factor are negligible, leaving an upper partial-product barrier together with a large terminal smooth-product condition. Derandomization turns those restrictions into a Gaussian walk constrained below an upper barrier and ending in a high window. The ballot estimate supplies separate path-survival and endpoint-window savings; after returning from |zeta|^2 mass to |zeta|, these yield the characteristic (log log T)^(-3/4) scale.
source_support: Units u06 and u21 give the Cauchy rectangle, split its sides into approximation error, small-smooth, and large-smooth regimes, and reduce the last regime to Key Proposition 4. Unit u18 proves the averaged fourth-moment bound with V^-2 saving and log T/log P rough loss; it is not a pointwise implication. Units u20 and u25 encode both upper partial-product and lower terminal restrictions and transfer them to a random expectation. Unit u19 proves the Gaussian ballot bound with one survival factor and two endpoint-window factors, while u24 applies it after conditioning away the tiny-prime block.
nonparaphrase_operation: Compose one-sided bridges and track what each preserves: evaluation at an argmax -> contour mass; total product largeness -> negligible small-smooth contribution in average; Euler-product restrictions -> random-walk barrier plus endpoint; ballot probabilities -> maximum upper-tail scale. The composition explains the 3/4 correction while refusing to invert any bridge.
limits: The fourth-moment step only controls an averaged exceptional contribution and does not force every large product to have a large smooth factor. Cauchy localization and positive integration discard concentration information, so the argument supplies no lower tail. The proved result is an upper tail with iterated-log factors; the full FHK centered distribution and matching lower bound remain conjectural. The Gaussian estimate is invoked through the random representation, and rectangle sizes, V dependence, barrier levels, U ranges, and log exponents are OCR-sensitive.
quality_reason: Accepted because the contour localization, fourth-moment largeness transfer, dual barrier construction, and Gaussian ballot estimate occur in distinct parents and form a verifiable one-way mechanism. The synthesis corrects the candidate's potentially pointwise word 'forces' to the averaged statement actually proved.

synthesis: The source traces much of the non-sharp iterated-log loss to a single coarse export of largeness across the smooth/rough split. Lemma 5 gains V^-2 when the smooth factor is small but pays the rough fourth-moment ratio log T/log P, forcing an overly large V and lowering the effective maximum threshold. The proposed repair is to replace one split by several successive prime bands: first transfer largeness to a smooth-plus-intermediate product with a smaller rough remainder, then use the already-known smooth lower condition to constrain the intermediate band, repeating if necessary. This is a source-authored resolution hierarchy and not a proved improvement.
source_support: Unit u04 identifies crude large-prime treatment and the overly large V as a primary source of extraneous log-log-log factors in Theorem 2. Units u06 and u18 locate and quantify that loss in the restricted fourth-moment transfer. Unit u07 explicitly proposes an intermediate band, possibly a growing number of bands, so successive transfers may incur smaller losses, while stating that no details were checked. Unit u08 independently shows why stronger rough-factor information is also needed to turn integrated mass into one extreme for a lower bound.
nonparaphrase_operation: Run a proof-level counterfactual: replace the one-shot binary factorization by a filtration of prime bands and ask at each stage which largeness implication, moment cost, and residual uncertainty would be carried forward. This explains how finer resolution might localize the loss without claiming the ledger closes.
limits: No multi-band argument, parameter choice, reduced-loss estimate, or sharp theorem is proved. The author calls the modification plausible and says order-one sharpness would also require substantial new probabilistic work. Even a successful upper-tail refinement would not automatically solve the lower-bound obstruction, since integrated mass can arise from several moderate values and the rough factor remains poorly localized. Exact V powers, band cutoffs, and logarithmic factors are OCR-sensitive.
quality_reason: Accepted as an explicitly source-supported speculative refinement, not as a theorem: u04/u18 diagnose the concrete loss, u07 proposes the multi-band response and disclaims verification, and u08 supplies an independent boundary on what that response would need to recover. The synthesis preserves all three epistemic statuses.
